title: The ladder of love
hook: Diotima teaches Socrates that love climbs from one beautiful person to beauty itself (Symposium 210–211)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was chesed, loyal, steady kindness. Your line was many words. Today, one more Greek word, and a staircase.

A dinner party in Athens, in Plato's Symposium. The guests agree to go easy on the wine and take turns giving speeches in praise of love. When it's Socrates' turn, the famous talker does something odd: he doesn't offer his own view. A wise woman from Mantinea named Diotima taught him what love is, he says, and he simply passes her lesson on. It has a shape, and the shape is a climb.
screen: `A DINNER PARTY IN ATHENS.` → `SOCRATES PASSES IT ON.` → `DIOTIMA OF MANTINEA.`

segments.voice: First, one beautiful person. The Greek word all night is eros, love as longing, love that wants what it doesn't yet have. Diotima says this love often begins with one beautiful person, and the lover is moved to speak beautiful words. Second, beauty in others. The lover notices that the beauty in one body is akin to the beauty in another, and the love widens past a single face. Third, beauty of soul: the beauty of minds and character, then of good laws and ways of living, then of knowledge. Fourth, beauty itself. At the top, Diotima says, the lover suddenly sees a beauty that doesn't grow or fade, isn't lovely in one way and ugly in another, and is the source of every beautiful thing below it. Readers call it the ladder of love, because she describes going up as if by steps. Some hear it as climbing away from people. Others hear the first love as the bottom rung: not thrown away, and without it there's no ladder at all. Plato leaves room for both readings. What's plain in the text is the direction: love, for Diotima, keeps reaching past the thing it started with.
screen: `ONE BEAUTIFUL PERSON.` · `BEAUTY IN OTHERS.` · `BEAUTY OF SOUL.` · `BEAUTY ITSELF.` · then, large: `THE LADDER OF LOVE.`

segments.voice: Let your eyes rest on something beautiful near you, or bring one to mind: a face, a line of music, a kind act you once saw, an idea that made you sit up. After a few breaths, let your attention climb one step and ask what it is in this that lifts you, not the thing itself but its beauty. If nothing comes, stay on the first rung; it's part of the ladder too.
Eros. Love as longing, the force in Plato's Symposium that climbs, step by step, from one beautiful person toward beauty itself. Today's word.
Your line: the ladder. The first rung counts too, and so does the climb. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Readers of Plato's Symposium, in philosophy classes and in some mystical writing shaped by Plato, discuss Diotima's ascent from the love of one person to the love of beauty itself.

notes: All of Plato is paraphrased (Jowett 1871 is public domain but not on the validator's list); consider adding Jowett to the list so short lines can be quoted.
Order of the ascent (one body, all bodies, souls, laws and practices, knowledge, beauty itself) follows 210a–211c; confirm.
'Readers call it the ladder' and 'as if by steps': Diotima's image of steps is at 211c; confirm.
The two readings (leaving the first love behind vs. standing on it) are described without ranking; confirm fairness.
